title: Treat Content Like a Nightclub: The Algorithm Is the Bouncer, and Your Only Job Is to Get Let In
dek: Kate Tolo spent five years taking Brian Johnson from 2,000 followers to tens of millions, and her core metaphor is this: the algorithm is a nightclub bouncer who only cares whether the people inside are having a good time — and you can fail a hundred times without anyone seeing.
why: This episode has medium information density, but Kate breaks her content methodology into 11 executable rules, with real emails, tweets and thumbnail examples — worth hearing for anyone doing content or brand work.
who: People doing content, brand or growth, especially creators and founders trying to build a personal IP or product brand from zero to one.
skip: The Shopify ad at the start and the chat about going public with a relationship at the end can be skipped.

points.h: The algorithm is a bouncer, not an enemy
points.body: Kate imagines the platform as a nightclub: only when the people inside are having a good time does the bouncer (the algorithm) let you in. Your only job is to understand what the bouncer wants — high-emotion, high-engagement content, whether that's hope, sadness, shock or education. She stresses the exchange is fair: you don't need to worry about follower count, posting time or how many times you post, only about making content that lets the people inside have a good time. And failure is invisible — you can try a hundred times and no one sees you get rejected.

points.h: Every platform is a different nightclub
points.body: Kate says the New York Times homepage, the iPhone App Store and the Uber Eats homepage recommendation slots are all nightclubs — all A/B testing for a limited number of seats, all fighting for your attention. So the same piece of content can't be moved as-is to every platform, because each nightclub's "ticket price" is different: on YouTube it's the title plus thumbnail, in email it's the subject line, in an app notification it's the first three words, on Twitter it's the tweet itself. You have to know which nightclub you're in before deciding what to wear.

points.h: Write the text first, then think about visuals
points.body: Kate insists on "start in text first": if the text story doesn't hold up, visualizing it only makes it messier. She gives the example of Blueprint's product photography — if you start by thinking "shoot the product", you might just put it on a white wall; but if you start with the story "this is a science experiment", you'll shoot the capsules in a petri dish as the container. Colin adds that they only recently started using reference images, and just "saying out loud what you want to shoot" changed the shoot results dramatically.

points.h: The three-step writing method: be clear, give value, pick the gossip
points.body: Kate's writing process has three steps: first, say what you want to say in the simplest words possible, ignoring marketing; second, rewrite it and ask "what value can I create for the person listening"; third, find the most "gossipy", most shareable element in that text and move it to the front. She stresses that "gossipy" doesn't have to be lowbrow — for example, "90% of visible skin aging comes from UV" is a shareable scientific fact.

points.h: After creating fear, you must immediately give a solution
points.body: Kate uses "90% of visible skin aging comes from everyday sun" as an example: the sentence creates fear and tension, but you can't leave fear hanging — you must immediately give an executable solution (say, three sun-protection rules), so the audience feels you're on their side and that the value you create is greater than the attention you ask for. She compares two tweets: one piles up research jargon ("a 2020 study of 161,286 people in Korea..."), the other is Brian's direct instruction ("brush your teeth immediately when you wake up") — the latter is what "speaking human" means.

points.h: The same sentence can be posted for a year
points.body: Kate shows two tweets exactly one year apart with identical content: "Sleep is the most powerful drug for improving performance, mental health and well-being." The first got 220,000 views, the second 348,000. She says people always assume they have to say something new every time, but if you have a good line, say it again and again. She mentions Blueprint wrote about 200 pieces of content about sleep, with no deliberate spacing needed — if it's good, post it again. Colin admits one of their biggest flaws is always wanting to reinvent the wheel.

points.h: Translate research into "do you want a cat or a dog"
points.body: Kate compares an academic paper title ("Protective effect of dog ownership on disabling dementia in older Japanese community residents") with Brian's tweet: "Do you want a cat or a dog? I want a dog and I exercise, dementia risk down 63%; I want a dog but don't exercise, zero benefit; I want a cat, zero benefit." She says this is what makes research "dead simple" — not simplification, but turning it into a multiple-choice question everyone wants to retweet. Colin says it reminds him of phone ads: nobody cares about the Snapdragon chip, they just want to know "call your mom".

points.h: Use "yes and" to turn haters into your own people
points.body: Kate says when Brian faces negative comments, he doesn't argue back — he "yes ands": agree with the other person first, then play along. For example, when someone mocked him for taking methylene blue, he went along with it and said "I was moved by the Smurfs movie"; when someone suggested "we need an anti-Brian Johnson: sleeps four hours, eats fast food, drinks and smokes but has perfect biomarkers", Brian posted a meme comparing himself with Liver King. Kate says this turns both positive and negative energy into your own energy, turning onlookers into "your own people".

terms.def: Kate's metaphor for the algorithm: it decides who gets into the traffic pool and only cares whether the users inside are having a good time.
The moment each platform's users decide whether to click your content: on YouTube it's the title plus thumbnail, in email it's the subject line.
The improv-comedy "yes, and": instead of arguing with negative comments, accept the other person's premise first, then play along, converting attack energy into your own traffic.

Start in text first because if you can perfect the text storytelling, everything becomes...
